entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Shuliang He (died 547 BCE), also known by his courtesy name Kong He, was a distinguished scholar-official and formidable military officer during the tumultuous Spring and Autumn period in the ancient Chinese State of Lu. His primary historical significance stems from his paternity of Kong Qiu, better known as Confucius, whose philosophical teachings would profoundly shape East Asian civilization for millennia. A scion of the influential Kong clan, Shuliang He navigated the complex political landscape of a fragmented China, where regional states vied for supremacy and internal factions constantly challenged central authority.

As a respected figure within the Lu aristocracy, Shuliang He held administrative posts and earned renown for his martial prowess. Records describe him as a man of exceptional strength and courage, notably during the siege of Bi in 563 BCE. When the city gate was lowered prematurely, trapping Lu forces, Shuliang He reportedly held the massive portcullis aloft with sheer physical power, allowing his besieged comrades to escape. This act of heroism cemented his reputation, reflecting the ideal of the warrior-scholar prevalent among the noble class of the time. He was also instrumental in defending the city of Fang, demonstrating strategic acumen alongside his physical might.

Shuliang He's most enduring legacy, however, is inextricably linked to his son, Confucius. Although he died when Confucius was only three years old, Shuliang He's noble lineage and the social standing he achieved provided the foundational context for Confucius's upbringing and subsequent intellectual development. The values of duty, martial virtue, and public service that characterized Shuliang He's life likely influenced the nascent philosophical inquiries of his son, contributing indirectly to the ethical and political framework that would become Confucianism, a cornerstone of Chinese thought and governance.
